blocks.text: Coffee reached Istanbul from Yemen in the middle of the 16th century, first in the palace and the houses of the rich. Public coffeehouses followed in the 1550s: two men from Syria, Hakem from Aleppo and Şems from Damascus, are said to have opened the first one, in the Tahtakale district.

The *kahvehane* (coffeehouse) soon became the place where men met to talk, read, listen to storytellers and hear the news. Not every ruler liked it: Sultan Murad IV ordered the coffeehouses closed in 1633, but bans like his never lasted long.

Turkish coffee is ground as fine as flour and cooked, not filtered. Coffee, cold water and sugar go together into a small long-handled pot, the *cezve*, which heats slowly until a thick foam, the *köpük*, rises. The coffee is poured, foam first, into a small cup, the *fincan*, where the grounds settle at the bottom. It comes with a glass of water, and often with a piece of *lokum*.
Because the sugar is cooked with the coffee, you choose it when you order: *sade* (plain, no sugar), *az şekerli* (a little sugar), *orta* (medium) or *şekerli* (sweet).

Coffee belongs to hospitality and to the big moments of life. When a family visits to ask for a young woman's hand in marriage, the *kız isteme*, she makes and serves the coffee; tradition says she may put salt instead of sugar in the groom's cup to test his patience. After drinking, some people turn the cup upside down on its saucer and read the shapes in the grounds: the *kahve falı*, coffee fortune-telling.

In 2013 UNESCO added Turkish coffee culture and tradition to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its description stresses what the coffee is for more than how it tastes: conversation, friendship and hospitality, in coffeehouses and at home, at engagements and on holidays. Coffee even gave its name to breakfast, *kahvaltı*, as you saw in [unit 8](a1-u08-culture).

blocks.en: A cup of coffee is remembered for forty years.

blocks.text: Here is an order at a coffeehouse in the Turkish of this unit:

lines.en: Please, have a seat. What would you like?

lines.tr: İki kahve, lütfen. Bir sade, bir de orta.
lines.en: Two coffees, please. One plain and one medium.
Thanks. And please don't forget the water!
